strengths: Clearly motivated and well-written position/framework paper that identifies a genuine gap: most LLM UQ research targets static, single-turn QA while deployed agents operate in long-horizon, interactive settings.

The unified formulation (Sec. 3.2) is genuinely useful as a taxonomy: mapping existing aggregation schemes (sum, max, weighted average, length-normalized, tail confidence, process reward modeling) as special cases of a chain-rule decomposition of trajectory uncertainty provides real conceptual clarity and a serviceable vocabulary for the field.

The graphical model (Fig. 2) and Definition 1/2 cleanly generalize many agent benchmark setups (function calling, ReAct, Reflexion in Appendix A), and the connections to probabilistic Turing machines and POMDP belief tracking (Appendix C) are thoughtfully drawn with honest discussion of the differences.

The core conceptual claim — that agent uncertainty is not monotone because interactive, information-seeking actions can reduce uncertainty — is intuitive, well illustrated (Fig. 3), and likely to stimulate useful discussion.

Honest and substantive limitations and open-problems sections (unreliable observations, black-box estimation cost, solution multiplicity, calibration), and the appendix is unusually thorough (alternative entropy measures, implementation notes, missing proof).
weaknesses: No empirical validation whatsoever. The central claim that existing UQ methods fail the desideratum (Eq. 1) on real agent trajectories is supported only by a single hand-constructed anecdote (Fig. 3a). A small experiment on tau-bench showing that gated estimates better predict trajectory reward than sum/max/mean baselines would have been straightforward and is conspicuously absent.

The formal contribution is thin. The 'conditional uncertainty reduction process' amounts to multiplying turn-level uncertainties by a hand-signed gating function; Lemma 1 follows almost immediately from monotone summation of the gated terms. The derivation in Appendix F is essentially definitional.

The proposal conflates uncertainty quantification with reward expectation. The desideratum (Eq. 1) asks uncertainty to be predictive of success, but the paper's mechanism achieves this by assigning negative uncertainty contributions to 'interactive and evidential' actions based on a classifier's judgment of action type — this bakes in a policy preference (interactivity is good) rather than measuring epistemic uncertainty, and the resulting 'uncertainty' can become negative, undermining its interpretation as an uncertainty measure.

Key quantities required by the framework are acknowledged to be very hard to estimate (mutual information between observation and initial query given history, observation uncertainty without world access), and the implementation is left entirely to future work ('Sketch of implementation'), so the actionable value of the framework remains untested.

The 'first general formulation' claim is overstated: recent work the paper itself cites (e.g., Kirchhof et al., 2025b position paper; UProp; Zhao et al., 2025) already treats uncertainty in agentic, multi-step settings, so the incremental novelty over that line is limited to the gating perspective.
Typos and polish issues (e.g., 'determistic' p.5, 'Relible' in Sec. 5.4 heading, 'randon varaibles' in Appendix A.1) suggest insufficient proofreading for a main-track submission.

Reproducibility is moot in the code sense (nothing to run), but the paper also does not specify how the dichotomous action classification (interactive/evidential) should be evaluated for consistency, which is where most practical brittleness would arise.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: extending uncertainty quantification from static single-turn LLM QA to interactive, multi-turn agent settings addresses a genuine gap in the literature, and the paper correctly identifies that trajectory-level uncertainty in open environments is not well served by existing pointwise or uni-directional propagation methods.

The unified formulation (Sec. 3) is a reasonable contribution: casting prior UQ setups (single-step LLM UQ, multi-step reasoning UQ, process reward modeling) as special cases of a chain-rule decomposition over a stochastic agent trajectory is a clean and pedagogically useful organization of a scattered literature.

The paper is clearly written and well structured, with an explicit desideratum (Eq. 1), a concrete graphical model, worked reductions to existing setups, and appendices covering alternative uncertainty measures, action taxonomies across benchmarks, and connections to POMDPs and probabilistic Turing machines.
The discussion of open problems (benchmarks, black-box estimation, solution multiplicity, multi-agent settings) is thoughtful and could usefully guide follow-up work.
weaknesses: No empirical validation whatsoever. This is a purely conceptual paper, but it is not framed as a formal position paper; it makes substantive technical claims (e.g., that existing methods fail the desideratum Eq. 1) that are supported only by a single hypothetical illustrative example (Fig. 3). No experiments, simulations, or even small-scale case studies on τ-bench or ToolSandbox are provided, despite the paper itself repeatedly invoking these benchmarks.

The core proposed mechanism, the information-gating function g(·), is heuristic and unverifiable as presented. It depends on classifying actions as 'interactive and evidential' (requiring a compound classifier whose errors are never analyzed), and on estimating conditional mutual information between free-form observations and the initial query — an estimation problem the paper itself acknowledges is 'notorious' — yet leaves all implementation 'for future work.' The gate can produce negative turn-uncertainty contributions whose behavior under realistic, noisy estimation is not characterized.

The mathematical contribution is thin. Eq. 6 is essentially an equality rewritten with the gate inserted, not a derived bound in any meaningful sense, and Lemma 1 follows almost immediately from monotonicity assumptions rather than from substantive analysis. Calling this 'analytic bounds' overstates the result.

The claim of presenting 'the first general formulation of agent UQ' is overstated; the related work cites Kirchhof et al. (2025b), a position paper explicitly arguing that UQ for LLM agents needs reassessment, and POMDP belief-tracking and information-theoretic treatments of active inference already cover much of the conceptual ground. The paper's differentiation from these (Appendix C) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The desideratum (Eq. 1) is never instantiated or tested: no uncertainty function, no reward model, no trajectories, no correlation analysis. As the paper's own open-problems section admits, calibrated evaluation is the hard part — which makes a framework paper that defers all of it difficult to assess for soundness or usefulness.

Reproducibility is effectively nil: there is no method to reimplement, no released artifacts, and the sketch of implementation lists four quantities whose estimation strategies are only name-checked with citations.

Minor but telling issues: a typo in a section title ('Relible Embodied Agents'), citations to unpublished/anonymous future work (ICLR 2026), and heavy reliance on arXiv preprints for core claims, which weakens the evidentiary grounding.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated position: the argument that UQ for LLMs must account for interactivity and reducible uncertainty in agentic, open-world settings is compelling and clearly articulated (Figure 1 contrast is effective).

The formal setup (Definition 1, dynamic Bayesian network over actions/observations/environment states) is clean, and Sec. 3.2 does a genuine service by showing how diverse prior UQ methods (pointwise, min-step, length-normalized, tail-confidence, PRM-style aggregation) arise as special cases of one trajectory-level uncertainty expansion.

The conditional uncertainty reduction perspective with an information-gating function is a novel and conceptually appealing re-framing, and Lemma 1 provides closed-form extrema that give the proposal some theoretical substance.

Good scholarly context: the paper situates itself against POMDP belief tracking and probabilistic Turing machines (Appendix C), covers related work thoroughly, and is candid about assumptions and open problems (benchmarks, black-box estimation, solution multiplicity, multi-agent settings).
Practical implications (healthcare, software engineering, embodied agents) and implementation notes in Appendix D make the framework actionable for practitioners rather than purely abstract.
weaknesses: No empirical evidence whatsoever for the central empirical claim. The key argument that existing UQ methods 'fail the desiderata' on agent trajectories rests on a single anecdotal case study (Fig. 3a). A small-scale experiment on τ-bench trajectories showing that trajectory-level uncertainty fails to predict reward (Eq. 1) would substantially strengthen the paper; as written, the limitation claim is asserted, not demonstrated.

The formal contribution is thinner than it appears: the uncertainty expansion is a direct application of the chain rule, and Lemma 1's proof (Appendix F) is essentially trivial given the definitions. The gating function's inequality direction in Eq. 6 and the mixed sign semantics are not rigorously justified and are hard to verify; the 'lower bound' claim deserves more careful treatment.

Strong simplifying assumptions (deterministic environment update, reliable observations, correct action classification) limit realism; the acknowledgments in Limitations are appropriate but mean the framework applies to only a narrow slice of real agent deployments.

Key quantities required by the framework (observation uncertainty, initial query uncertainty, conditional mutual information between observations and queries) are acknowledged to be very difficult to estimate, and the paper defers all implementation to future work. This makes the 'actionable guidance' claim weak — the operational path is largely speculative.

Novelty positioning relative to Kirchhof et al. (2025b), which already argues UQ needs reassessment for LLM agents, and prior interactive/agentic UQ work (Chan et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2025; Frankel et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025) could be sharpened; the claim of being the 'first general formulation' is an overstatement given these precedents.

Polish issues remain: several typos ('Relible', 'determistic', 'randon varaibles'), and the desideratum (Eq. 1) is stated informally without discussion of how strict monotonicity in expectation should be tested or measured.
